tagline: Fishing boats, sandstone bays and estate gardens on the road to Bandon
intro: The Charleston-Bandon Tour Route leaves the Pacific Coast Scenic Byway for fishing-port waterfronts, sandstone cliffs and a cape above the ocean. ODOT describes a 41-mile tour with a minimum driving time of two to three hours, linking six state parks, two national wildlife refuges and the country’s first National Estuarine Research Reserve. The Cape Arago leg ends 200 feet above the Pacific and requires a six-mile retrace before the southbound turn onto Seven Devils Road.

Along this coast, private holdings became public parks. Shore Acres began as timber baron Louis Simpson’s estate in 1910. After fire and financial losses, he sold it to Oregon in 1942; state restoration of the gardens began in 1970. At Sunset Bay, Coos County donated the first park tract in 1948, with later additions enlarging it. South Slough followed in 1974 as the first reserve created in response to the federal Coastal Zone Management Act of 1972.

From North Bend, follow Cape Arago Highway through Charleston, then past Sunset Bay and Shore Acres to Cape Arago. After the retrace, Seven Devils Road leads south past South Slough and cranberry bogs. The southern leg takes in Coquille River Lighthouse and skirts Bandon Marsh National Wildlife Refuge before ending in Bandon’s Old Town.

moments.title: Sunset Bay State Park
moments.text: A crescent beach and sandstone cliffs give Sunset Bay its shape. Along the shoreline, stumps of drowned spruce trees record a much older change. An earthquake on the Cascadia subduction zone lowered the shore about 1,200 years ago, creating this ghost forest. The park itself grew in stages: Coos County donated its original tract in 1948, and Ralph Barker added land with a water supply in 1954. A hiking trail links Sunset Bay with neighboring Shore Acres. The University of Oregon began its marine biology program here in 1924, teaching and researching from tents along the beach.

moments.title: Shore Acres State Park
moments.text: Five acres of formal gardens occupy the former Simpson estate above the Pacific. A rose-testing plot and Japanese lily pond are among their features. Timber baron Louis Simpson built the estate in 1910, but a 1921 fire and financial losses preceded his sale to Oregon in 1942. During World War II the property served as an Army radar station, with its buildings used as barracks. Those buildings were demolished after the war. Garden restoration began in 1970; the gardens are now open to the public. Plants from across the world grow in the estate gardens on this ocean bluff.
moments.notice: The formal gardens include a rose-testing plot and a Japanese lily pond.

moments.title: Bandon
moments.text: George Bennett gave Bandon the name of his County Cork hometown and introduced gorse to the area. The spiny plant spread through the town and countryside. In September 1936, a forest fire swept into Bandon and destroyed its entire commercial district. Resident D.H. Woomer told The Coos Bay Times that the forest fire had ignited the town’s abundant gorse. Before the fire, part of that district stood on wooden pilings over the Coquille River, with river traffic reaching merchants’ doors. Rebuilding kept the business district within the available land.
